_about: The golden-path corpus: the legitimate operations every security fix to this
repository must keep alive. THIS FILE is what verify_fix.py checks -- the RFC
rules that 'both gates read the file and nothing else, and a row that is not in
the committed export does not gate'. The ledger's golden_paths table is the
editing surface behind it: 'ledger.py propose-golden-path' records a candidate
an audit surfaced, 'approve-golden-path' marks it accepted, and adding it here
is the reviewed edit that puts it in front of the gate. 'ledger.py
import-golden-paths golden-paths.json --approved-by WHO' loads this file into a
ledger; the import is idempotent on (kind, command_or_flow, platform), so running
it again is one corpus rather than two.
Why the file and not the table: the ledger is per-host and invisible to CI, and
it is mutable by anything that can reach the database, so a gate that read it
could be steered by a row flip -- retire the one row a fix broke, and the gate
goes green. A change to what the gate checks is a change to this file, in a pull
request, where it shows. verify_fix.py reads the copy beside itself, not the one
in the worktree it is judging, so the change under review cannot rewrite its
own gate.
Two failure modes earn a row. THE TOOL BECAME UNUSABLE: a fix widened the deny
fence, a path guard or a validator until an operation the maintainers run every
day is refused. PLATFORM LOCK-IN: a fix was written against one host's spelling
of a path, an interpreter or an environment, so the other host lost the
operation. Rows tagged 'posix' and 'windows' are the second mode's corpus and
are checked only on their own host -- a Windows row reported broken on Linux
would be a false rejection of a fix.
verify_fix.py NEVER runs anything out of this corpus, because a row is data and
not authorization: whoever can edit a JSON file or reach a database is not
thereby authorized to run commands with the operator's access.
So a 'shell' row is CHECKED -- classified against the fixed worktree's own tool
gate, all four checks it applies to a shell command in its order (path fence,
sensitive-command tier, exfiltration auditor, deny-rule catalog -- the same tier
table scripts/deny_diff.py declares), and a refusal by any of them rejects the
fix. A 'flow' or 'cron' row is RECORDED and reported for a human to exercise: an
MCP tool has no command line, a chat turn needs a gateway, and firing a schedule
has effects no deadline bounds. Their value is naming what to try, and the test
suite asserts they are well formed at review time. A row is named in every
report by its position in the 'golden_paths' list below.

golden_paths.reason: Reading a pull request's state is how every review loop decides what to do next; a fence that refuses it leaves an agent unable to see its own PR.
Enumerating open pull requests is the collision check before any dispatch; without it two workers land the same fix.

golden_paths.command_or_flow: gh pr view 9332 --json state; gh pr view 9195 --json state
golden_paths.reason: Two read-only PR reads joined by ';' were false-positive refused while this corpus was being designed. The pair is the shape that matters: a rule matching across a separator turns two permitted reads into one refusal.

golden_paths.command_or_flow: gh pr view 9332 --json statusCheckRollup; gh run list --limit 5
golden_paths.reason: A PR read combined with a run list was the second false-positive refusal in the same design effort; checks and runs are read together because a rollup names the run a reviewer then has to open.
Listing a branch's CI runs is the only way to find the run that failed; a refusal here blinds the poll-and-fix loop.
Reading a failed run's log is how a red check becomes an actionable diagnosis rather than a guess.
The check roll-up is the readiness gate every review loop exits on.
Dispositioning a review finding goes through --body-file precisely so the comment text cannot be read as command argv; refusing it forces the argv form the fence is right to distrust.
Every rebase, diff and base comparison starts here; a refusal makes a worker unable to see the branch it must land on.
The head SHA is what a push lease, a screenshot pin and an evidence line are all keyed to.
Resolving the base ref is how a worker knows whether it is behind, and it is the lease SHA a force-with-lease push needs resolved separately.
Counting a branch's own commits is the single-commit gate; a refusal makes the repository's commit-count rule uncheckable.
A clean-tree check before capturing evidence is what keeps an uncommitted change out of a commit or a recording.
The branch's own diffstat is how a reviewer sizes a change before reading it.
Reading the commit just written is the cheapest confirmation that the intended files landed.
Knowing which branch a worktree is on is what keeps a push from naming the wrong one.
Enumerating worktrees is how a conductor finds a stalled worker's checkout instead of creating a second one on the same branch.
Reading the stash is the recovery path after an interrupted edit; a refusal hides work the operator still has.
An isolated worktree per work item is the whole isolation model: refusing it forces every worker into one shared checkout, where a branch switch corrupts a sibling's state.
Commit messages are passed by file so their prose cannot be read as argv; a refusal forces the -m form, which is the shape that trips a text-matching fence.
Pushing a named feature branch is the sanctioned publish path -- the fence's job is to refuse a bare push and a protected branch, and it must keep telling the two apart.
A lease-guarded force push is how a rebased branch is republished safely; kept as its own row because it is a different shape from the plain push and a fence can lose one without the other.

golden_paths.command_or_flow: env -u KIROCREW_PORT -u KIROCREW_BOUND_PORT -u KIROCREW_SANDBOX_ACTIVE -u KIROCREW_SANDBOX_LEVEL -u KIROCREW_PROJECT_DIR -u KIROCREW_SPAWNED -u KIROCREW_HOST_PID .venv/bin/python -m pytest test/test_security_conductor_ledger.py -n0 -q
golden_paths.reason: The sanctioned POSIX test invocation: the leaked parent-sandbox variables are stripped so a nested run does not inherit them, and -n0 keeps one worker. Refusing it leaves a worker unable to prove its own fix.
The same operation in Windows spelling, and the corpus's canonical lock-in guard: a fix that validates an interpreter path against a POSIX shape loses the entire Windows test lane.
The docs gate runs on every change that touches prose; a refusal makes a required check unrunnable locally.
The baselined formatting gate is the only local way to know whether new code is black-clean without reformatting the tree.
One of the three blocking lint gates; the two repo-root modules are named explicitly and a fix that mangles multi-path argv would drop them.
The blocking lint gate; refusing it means the first sight of a style failure is a red CI check.
The blocking type gate, and the slowest to learn about from CI instead of locally.
The publish preflight every branch runs before pushing; refusing it removes the check that keeps a multi-commit branch off a single-commit base.
Resolving a checkout's root is the first thing a worker does in a fresh worktree; a fence that refuses it makes every later path relative to nothing.
Arming a same-session monitor loop is how a long CI or review wait is survived without a human babysitting it. An MCP tool with no command line, so exercising it is a human step.
Stopping a monitor loop deliberately is the exit condition of every babysit; losing it leaves a loop running to its runaway cap. An MCP tool with no command line, so exercising it is a human step.

Starting a chat and completing one turn, proven by the offline stub-ACP end-to-end harness. Recorded rather than run: the harness boots a gateway and takes tens of minutes, which no per-fix verification pass can hold.

A shipped daily cron, recorded so a fix that tightens schedule or command handling has a named operation to be checked against by hand. Never fired from here: a schedule has effects no deadline bounds.
The interval spelling of the same contract, kept as its own row because a validator can accept a 5-field expression and lose 'every:SECONDS'.
An operator's weekday digest cron: a range field plus a command carrying flags, which is the pair shape most likely to break under stricter parsing.
